summary: Proxy Mobile IPv6 requires mobile access gateways to use a fixed link-local and link-layer address on shared links, so a node sees no change when it roams. This RFC reserves an IPv6 interface identifier for that purpose.

eli5.summary: If your phone moves between helpers, it should think it is still talking to the same one. This sets aside one special address name that every helper can use.

questions: reserved ipv6 interface identifier proxy mobile ipv6
what is the reserved interface identifier for proxy mobile ipv6

what ethernet address does rfc 6543 reserve
subtitle: Reserves a fixed Ethernet address and IPv6 interface identifier for Proxy Mobile IPv6 gateways.

tldr.problem: RFC 5213 requires all mobile access gateways to use a fixed link-local and link-layer address, but reserved no addresses, which proved an operational challenge with multi-vendor equipment.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6543 reserves Ethernet address 00-00-5E-00-52-13 and the IPv6 interface identifier 0200:5EFF:FE00:5213 derived from it.
tldr.outcome: Gateways SHOULD use these on all shared access links, so a mobile node sees no change when it roams between gateways.

today: RFC 6543 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5213. No later RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Fixed Address Problem
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213) is a network-based mobility protocol that gives a mobile node IP mobility without the node taking part in any mobility signaling. The network ensures the node does not detect any change in its Layer 3 attachment, even after it roams from one mobile access gateway to another.

To do this, all gateways in a domain use a fixed link-local address and a fixed link-layer address on access links shared with mobile nodes. The base specification did not reserve any particular addresses, which is proving an operational challenge in multi-vendor deployments.
sections.eli5: The phone should not notice when it switches helpers, so all helpers must use the same address. But nobody had agreed on which one.

sections.title: The Two Reservations
sections.content:
First, one Ethernet unicast address, 00-00-5E-00-52-13, is reserved. Mobile access gateways SHOULD use it on all access links shared with mobile nodes, and the variable FixedMAGLinkLayerAddressOnAllAccessLinks SHOULD be set to it.

Second, the IPv6 interface identifier 0200:5EFF:FE00:5213 is reserved. It is a modified EUI-64 identifier generated from that Ethernet address. Gateways SHOULD use it on all shared access links, and FixedMAGLinkLocalAddressOnAllAccessLinks SHOULD be set to the link-local address built from it. The gateway can use that address in all Neighbor Discovery communication with the mobile node.
sections.eli5: Two special names are set aside: one for the physical address and one for the internet address built from it. Every helper uses the same two.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The Ethernet address was allocated from the "IANA Ethernet Address Block - Unicast Use" registry. The interface identifier is recorded in the "Reserved IPv6 Interface Identifiers" registry defined by RFC 5453, as generated per Appendix A of RFC 4291.
sections.eli5: The official lists now show these two names as taken, so nobody else will use them for something else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations in RFC 5213 and RFC 5844 continue to apply, including the issues with fixed link-local and link-layer addresses in Section 6.9.3 of RFC 5213.

The reservations make the same address values usable beyond a single domain, which widens the existing problem of asserting ownership of the addresses to a multi-domain environment. Future work may be needed.
sections.eli5: Because many networks now share the same special names, it is harder to prove who really owns one. People may need to solve that later.
